q-143789:
If $X$ is a discrete random variable with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S,$ the expected value of ${X}^{3}$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{3}]={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{3}\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each cubed value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{3}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{3}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={0}^{3}\cdot \frac{5}{18}+{1}^{3}\cdot \frac{2}{9}+{2}^{3}\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0\cdot \frac{5}{18}+1\cdot \frac{2}{9}+8\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0+\frac{2}{9}+4 \\  & =\frac{38}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-143827:
If $X$ is a discrete random variable with probability mass function $f(x)$ and sample space $S,$ the expected value of ${X}^{4}$ is given by

$$
\text{E}[{X}^{4}]={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{4}\cdot f(x).
$$

Summing up the products of each squared value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{4}] & ={\sum }_{x\in S}{x}^{4}\cdot f(x) \\  & ={1}^{4}\cdot 0.25+{2}^{4}\cdot 0.6+{3}^{4}\cdot 0.1+{4}^{4}\cdot 0.05 \\  & =1\cdot 0.25+16\cdot 0.6+81\cdot 0.1+256\cdot 0.05 \\  & =0.25+9.6+8.1+12.8 \\  & =30.75.\end{aligned}
$$

q-109312:
Expanding out the product inside the expected value, using the properties of the expected value, and substituting in the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X(3X-2)+4] & =\text{E}[3{X}^{2}-2X+4] \\  & =3\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]+\text{E}[4] \\  & =3\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-2\text{E}[X]+4 \\  & =3(27)-2(5)+4 \\  & =75.\end{aligned}
$$

q-110011:
Expanding out the square inside the expected value, using the properties of the expected value, and substituting in the given information, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[(2Y-8)^{2}] & =\text{E}[4{Y}^{2}-32Y+64] \\  & =4\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-32\text{E}[Y]+\text{E}[64] \\  & =4\text{E}[{Y}^{2}]-32\text{E}[Y]+64 \\  & =4(4)-32(1)+64 \\  & =48.\end{aligned}
$$

q-85596:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between two points where $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula:

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

In our case, $f(x)=\frac{8}{3}{x}^{3/2},$ $a=0,$ and $b=3.$

First, we find the derivative of $f(x):$

$$
{f}^{′}(x)=4\sqrt{x}
$$

Substituting ${f}^{′}(x)=4\sqrt{x}$ to the formula for the arc length, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+[4\sqrt{x}]^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\sqrt{1+16x}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We evaluate this integral using the substitution $u=1+16x.$ Then, $\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\text{d}u.$

We also need to compute new limits:

$$
\begin{aligned}x & 0 & 3 \\ u & 1 & 49\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{1}^{49}\sqrt{u}\cdot \frac{1}{16}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{16}{\int }_{1}^{49}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{16}{[\frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}]|}_{1}^{49} \\  & =\frac{1}{24}({49}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =\frac{343-1}{24} \\  & =\frac{57}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-122394:
The arc length of a curve $y=f(x)$ between $x=a$ and $x=b$ can be found using the formula

$$
L={\int }_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

We're given that 

$$
L={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\sqrt{1+\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Comparing the above with the arc length formula, we see that we must have

$$
[{f}^{′}(x)]^{2}=\frac{1}{{(1+{x}^{2})}^{2}}\,⟹\,{f}^{′}(x)=\pm \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}.
$$

Integrating the above equation with respect to $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\pm \int \frac{1}{1+{x}^{2}}\text{ d}x \\  & =\pm \operatorname{arctan}⁡x+C.\end{aligned}
$$

From the given options, the only one that has the required form is $y=\operatorname{arctan}⁡x-\pi .$

q-42106:
Using cofactor expansion along the third row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}| & =2\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2|\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2(1\cdot 1-2\cdot (-1)) \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
|\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}|=-2\cdot 6=-12.
$$

q-130035:
Using cofactor expansion along the third row, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =0\cdot {C}_{31}+2\cdot {C}_{32}+0\cdot {C}_{33}+0\cdot {C}_{34} \\  & =2\cdot (-1)^{3+2}\cdot |\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|\end{aligned}
$$

Now, computing the $3\times 3$ determinant by applying a Laplace expansion along the $1$st row, we obtain:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}4 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 5 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}| & =4\cdot {C}_{11}+0\cdot {C}_{12}+0\cdot {C}_{13} \\  & =4\cdot (-1)^{1+1}\cdot |\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4|\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -1 & 2\end{aligned}| \\  & =4(3\cdot 2-(-1)\cdot (-2)) \\  & =4\cdot 4 \\  & =16\end{aligned}
$$

$$
|\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 3 & -2 \\ 0 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 5 & 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}|=-2\cdot 16=-32.
$$

q-129108:
The variance of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

First, we need to compute the probability mass function $f(x).$ Here, there are $6$ possible outcomes ($-3,-1,2,3,5,12$) and each outcome has the same probability, so the probability mass function is as follows:

| $x$ | $-3$ | $-1$ | $2$ | $3$ | $5$ | $12$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $f(x)$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ | $\frac{1}{6}$ |

Now, we need to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =(-3)\cdot f(-3)+(-1)\cdot f(-1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+5\cdot f(5)+12\cdot f(12) \\  & =(-3)(\frac{1}{6})+(-1)(\frac{1}{6})+2(\frac{1}{6})+3(\frac{1}{6})+5(\frac{1}{6})+12(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=3$ into the variance formula, we get

$$
\text{Var}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}(x-3)^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

Now, we compute the variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =(-3-3)^{2}\cdot f(-3)+(-1-3)^{2}\cdot f(-1)+(2-3)^{2}\cdot f(2)+(3-3)^{2}\cdot f(3) \\  & +(5-3)^{2}\cdot f(5)+(12-3)^{2}\cdot f(12) \\  & =36\cdot f(-3)+16\cdot f(-1)+1\cdot f(2)+0\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(5)+81\cdot f(12) \\  & =36(\frac{1}{6})+16(\frac{1}{6})+1(\frac{1}{6})+0+4(\frac{1}{6})+81(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =23\end{aligned}
$$

q-84023:
The variance of a discrete random variable $X$ with probability mass function $f(x)$ defined over a set $S$ is given by

$$
\text{Var}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}(x-\text{E}[X])^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

First, we need to compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{3})+2(\frac{1}{4})+3(\frac{1}{6})+4(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $\text{E}[X]=\frac{7}{3}$ into the variance formula, we get

$$
\text{Var}[X]={\sum }_{x\in S}{(x-\frac{7}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(x).
$$

Now, we compute the variance as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & ={(1-\frac{7}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{(2-\frac{7}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{(3-\frac{7}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{(4-\frac{7}{3})}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =\frac{16}{9}\cdot f(1)+\frac{1}{9}\cdot f(2)+\frac{4}{9}\cdot f(3)+\frac{25}{9}\cdot f(4) \\  & =\frac{16}{9}(\frac{1}{3})+\frac{1}{9}\cdot (\frac{1}{4})+\frac{4}{9}\cdot (\frac{1}{6})+\frac{25}{9}(\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =\frac{25}{18}\end{aligned}
$$

q-84200:
We can compute the variance of a discrete random variable $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

First, we compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4)+5\cdot f(5)+6\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{8})+2(\frac{1}{4})+3(\frac{3}{8})+4(\frac{1}{16})+5(\frac{1}{8})+6(\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4)+{5}^{2}\cdot f(5)+{6}^{2}\cdot f(6) \\  & =1(\frac{1}{8})+4(\frac{1}{4})+9(\frac{3}{8})+16(\frac{1}{16})+25(\frac{1}{8})+36(\frac{1}{16}) \\  & =\frac{87}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{87}{8}-{3}^{2} \\  & =\frac{87}{8}-9 \\  & =\frac{15}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$

q-84208:
We can compute the variance of a discrete random variable $X$ using the following formula:

$$
\text{Var}[X]=\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2}
$$

First, we compute $\text{E}[X].$ Summing up the products of each value of $X$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[X] & =0\cdot f(0)+1\cdot f(1)+2\cdot f(2)+3\cdot f(3)+4\cdot f(4) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{6})+1(\frac{1}{9})+2(\frac{1}{3})+3(\frac{2}{9})+4(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{19}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we compute $\text{E}[{X}^{2}].$ Summing up the products of each value of ${X}^{2}$ and its associated probability, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{E}[{X}^{2}] & ={0}^{2}\cdot f(0)+{1}^{2}\cdot f(1)+{2}^{2}\cdot f(2)+{3}^{2}\cdot f(3)+{4}^{2}\cdot f(4) \\  & =0(\frac{1}{6})+1(\frac{1}{9})+4(\frac{1}{3})+9(\frac{2}{9})+16(\frac{1}{6}) \\  & =\frac{55}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Var}[X] & =\text{E}[{X}^{2}]-\text{E}[X]^{2} \\  & =\frac{55}{9}-{(\frac{19}{9})}^{2} \\  & =\frac{55}{9}-\frac{361}{81} \\  & =\frac{134}{81}.\end{aligned}
$$
